essays.stem: Explain what a business is, and describe the main types of business ownership, with an advantage and a disadvantage of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A business is an organisation that provides goods or services to customers, usually to make a profit. A hotel or villa sells services such as rooms, meals, tours and transfers. A sole trader is owned and run by one person, such as a woman who runs a small guest house. It is easy to set up and she keeps all the profit, but she carries all the risk, and her own savings could be lost if the business fails. A partnership is owned by two or more people who share the work, money and profit. They bring more skills and money, but they can disagree, and each partner can be responsible for the business's debts. A limited company is a separate legal body owned by shareholders. The owners' own money is protected if the company fails, and it is easier to raise money, but it must keep more records and follow more rules. A co-operative is owned and run by its members, such as craft vendors, who share the profits. Members have an equal say, but decisions can be slow.
markingPoints: Defines a business (goods or services, usually for profit), with a hospitality example
Sole trader, with an advantage and a disadvantage
Partnership, with an advantage and a disadvantage
Limited company, with an advantage (owners' money protected) and a disadvantage
Co-operative, with an advantage and a disadvantage

essays.stem: Describe the main departments of a hotel and what each one does.
essays.modelAnswer: The front office takes reservations, checks guests in and out, handles guest bills and payments, and answers questions; it is the centre of communication. Housekeeping cleans and prepares guest rooms and public areas, looks after linen and laundry, and reports maintenance problems and lost property. Food and beverage serves meals and drinks in the restaurant, bar, room service and events, and the kitchen plans the menus and prepares the food. Maintenance, or engineering, keeps the building, air conditioning, plumbing, electrics and pool in good working order. Security protects guests, staff and property, and controls who comes into the hotel. Sales and marketing promote the hotel, make deals with travel companies and bring in bookings and events. The accounts department handles the money: bills, payments to suppliers, payroll and records. Human resources recruits, trains and looks after the staff. In a small villa, a few people may cover several of these jobs. For example, the villa manager may handle bookings and accounts, while a housekeeper, cook, butler and gardener look after the guests and the property.
markingPoints: Front office and housekeeping, with correct duties
Food and beverage and the kitchen, with correct duties
Maintenance and security, with correct duties
Sales and marketing, accounts and human resources, with correct duties
Notes that in a small villa staff may cover several jobs

essays.stem: Explain how the departments of a hotel or villa must work together, using the example of a guest's stay from booking to check-out.
essays.modelAnswer: Each department depends on the others to give the guest a smooth stay. When a guest books, reservations record the dates, the room type and any special requests, such as a late arrival or a food allergy, and pass them on. Before arrival, the front office tells housekeeping which rooms are needed, and housekeeping cleans and checks them and reports when each room is ready, so that the guest is not kept waiting. The kitchen is told about the allergy and plans for it. At check-in, the front office gives the key and tells the bell staff, who take the bags to the room. During the stay, if the guest reports a broken air conditioner, the front office logs it and maintenance fixes it quickly, then the front office checks that the guest is happy. Restaurant and bar charges are sent to the guest's bill. At check-out, the front office settles the bill and accounts records the payment, and housekeeping is told that the room is empty. If information is not passed on, guests are let down, so clear communication is essential.
markingPoints: Booking details and special requests are recorded and passed on
Housekeeping prepares rooms and reports room status to the front office
Kitchen, bell staff and maintenance each play their part during the stay
Charges go to the bill; the front office settles it and accounts records it at check-out
Explains that clear communication between departments is essential

essays.stem: Explain the difference between income, expenses and profit, and describe ways that staff can help a hotel increase its income and control its costs.
essays.modelAnswer: Income is all the money a business receives, for example from room sales, meals, drinks, tours and laundry. Expenses are the costs of running the business, such as wages, food and drink, electricity, water, linen, cleaning supplies, repairs, rent and insurance. Profit is what is left when the expenses are taken away from the income. For example, if a villa earns J$900 000 in a month and its costs are J$650 000, the profit is J$250 000. If the expenses are more than the income, the business makes a loss. Staff can help increase income by giving excellent service, so that guests return and recommend the property, by suggesting extras such as tours or dessert, and by making sure every charge is put on the guest's bill. Staff can help control costs by following recipes and portion sizes, reducing food waste, switching off lights and air conditioning in empty rooms, reporting leaks, using cleaning chemicals at the correct dilution, looking after equipment and linen, and preventing theft. Every worker's actions affect the profit.
markingPoints: Income defined, with hotel examples
Expenses defined, with hotel examples
Profit = income − expenses, with a correct example (or a loss explained)
Ways staff increase income (service, suggesting extras, recording charges)
Ways staff control costs (portions, waste, energy, chemicals, care of equipment, theft)

essays.stem: Explain how the seasons and demand affect a Jamaican villa or hotel's business, and what the business can do in the low season.
essays.modelAnswer: Jamaica's tourist high season is roughly from December to April, when many visitors come to escape the winter in North America and Europe. Demand is high, so villas and hotels are often full, rates are at their highest, and more staff and stock are needed. The low season, roughly from late spring into the autumn, brings fewer visitors and includes the hurricane season. Occupancy and income fall, but many costs, such as wages, insurance and loan payments, stay the same. A business must plan for this. In the high season it should save money for the quieter months and keep standards high so that guests return. In the low season it can offer lower rates and special packages, target local Jamaican guests and nearby Caribbean markets, promote weddings, family reunions and conferences, and work with tour operators. It can use the quieter time for repairs, painting, deep cleaning and staff training, and plan rosters so that staff hours match the work. Watching bookings and planning ahead helps the business stay profitable all year.
markingPoints: High season (roughly December to April) brings high demand and rates, and needs more staff and stock
Low season brings fewer guests and less income, while fixed costs remain
Saves money and keeps standards high in the high season
Low-season actions: lower rates, packages, local and regional guests, events
Uses the quiet time for repairs, deep cleaning and training, and plans rosters

essays.stem: Describe how a hotel or villa markets itself to attract guests.
essays.modelAnswer: Marketing is how a hotel or villa finds guests and persuades them to book. First, the business must know its product and what makes it special, such as a sea view, a private chef or a quiet location, and its target market, for example couples, families or groups of friends. It sets prices that suit that market and the season, and decides where guests can book: its own website, online travel websites, travel agents and tour operators, or by phone and email. Promotion tells people about the property. This can include good photos and videos on the website and social media, special offers, advertising, and taking part in travel fairs. Online reviews are very important, so the villa encourages happy guests to write them and replies politely to every review. Repeat guests can be offered a welcome-back gift or a discount, and an email newsletter keeps in touch with them. Staff are part of marketing too, because every friendly greeting and well-cleaned room makes guests more likely to recommend the villa to others.
markingPoints: Knows the product and what makes it special
Knows the target market and sets suitable prices
Chooses where guests can book (website, online travel websites, agents, tour operators)
Promotion: photos, social media, offers, advertising and reviews
Keeps repeat guests, and notes that staff service is part of marketing

essays.stem: Explain why tourism is important to Jamaica's economy, and how a villa can support its local community.
essays.modelAnswer: Tourism is one of Jamaica's largest industries. Visitors spend foreign exchange, such as US dollars, which the country needs to pay for imports like fuel, food and machinery. Tourism creates many jobs, directly in hotels, villas, attractions and transport, and indirectly for farmers, fishermen, craft makers, taxi operators, entertainers and suppliers. The government collects taxes from tourism businesses and visitors, which help pay for roads, schools and health care. Tourism also brings airports, roads and other services that local people use too. A villa can support its local community by buying fresh fruit, vegetables and fish from local farmers and fishermen, and by using local tradespeople for repairs. It can recommend local tour guides, restaurants and craft markets to guests, and share Jamaican culture through food and music. It can hire and train people from the area, protect the environment by saving water and energy and getting rid of waste properly, and take part in community projects. When local people benefit from tourism, they welcome visitors, which helps the whole industry.
markingPoints: Earns foreign exchange
Creates direct and indirect jobs, with examples
Brings taxes and better infrastructure
The villa supports the community by buying local, using local services and recommending local businesses
Hires locally, protects the environment, and explains why community support helps tourism

essays.stem: Describe how a villa should control its stock of supplies, such as food, drinks, linen and guest amenities.
essays.modelAnswer: Stock control makes sure the villa has what it needs, when it needs it, without waste or theft. First, the villa sets a par level for each item, which is the amount that should always be in stock, for example enough sets of linen for each bed, and enough toilet rolls and guest soaps for a week. Stock is counted regularly, and anything below par is reordered from approved suppliers with a written order. When deliveries arrive, they are checked against the order and the invoice for quantity, quality, dates and temperatures, and any problem is recorded and reported. Stock is stored in the right place: dry goods off the floor in a clean, dry store, chilled food at 5 °C or below, and chemicals apart from food and linen. Older stock is used first (first in, first out). Store rooms are locked, and items are signed out, so that the villa knows where they go. Records of use help the manager spot waste or loss and plan the budget. Staff report damage, spoilage or missing items at once.
markingPoints: Sets par levels and counts stock regularly
Reorders from approved suppliers with written orders
Checks deliveries against the order and invoice for quantity, quality, dates and temperatures
Stores stock correctly and uses first in, first out
Locks stores, signs items out, keeps records, and reports loss or spoilage

essays.stem: Explain what a SWOT analysis is, and carry one out for a small villa.
essays.modelAnswer: A SWOT analysis is a simple way to look at a business and plan ahead. S is strengths and W is weaknesses: these are inside the business. O is opportunities and T is threats: these come from outside it. For a small villa near Negril, strengths might be its beach view, a cook who makes excellent Jamaican food, and many good online reviews. Weaknesses might be an old website, only three bedrooms, and no staff who speak Spanish or French. Opportunities might be a new direct flight bringing more visitors, more interest in beach weddings, and local visitors on public holidays. Threats might be hurricanes, a big new hotel nearby with lower prices, and rising electricity costs. After listing these, the owner uses them to plan: build on the strengths, fix the weaknesses (for example with a new website), take up the opportunities (for example a wedding package), and prepare for the threats (insurance and a hurricane plan). A SWOT should be reviewed every year.
markingPoints: Explains SWOT: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Strengths and weaknesses are inside the business; opportunities and threats come from outside
Suitable strengths and weaknesses for a villa
Suitable opportunities and threats for a villa
Uses the analysis to plan actions, and reviews it

essays.stem: Explain how good customer service and quality standards affect the success of a hotel business.
essays.modelAnswer: In hospitality, the guest's experience is the product, so service and quality decide whether the business succeeds. When staff greet guests warmly, rooms are spotless, food is safe and tasty, and problems are solved quickly, guests are satisfied. Satisfied guests come back, recommend the property to friends and write good online reviews, which bring in new guests at little cost. They may also spend more on extras such as meals, tours and spa treatments. Quality standards, such as written procedures for cleaning a room or checking in a guest, make sure that every guest gets the same good standard, whoever is on duty. Poor service has the opposite effect: guests complain, ask for refunds, write bad reviews and do not return, so income falls. A good name also helps the property win business from tour operators and travel agents. Good service makes work more pleasant, and staff feel proud of what they do. For these reasons, every member of staff, from the gardener to the manager, plays a part in the success of the business.
markingPoints: The guest's experience is the product
Satisfied guests return, recommend the property and write good reviews
Satisfied guests spend more on extras
Written standards give every guest the same good quality
Poor service leads to complaints, refunds, bad reviews and lost income; every staff member plays a part

practical1.title: Hotel departments: an organisation chart and a guest's journey across the departments
practical1.brief: As a group, show how a small hotel or a large villa is organised and how its departments work together for one guest. Part 1: draw an organisation chart on chart paper for a 40-room hotel (or a villa, if the assessor chooses), showing the departments, the main job titles and who reports to whom. Part 2: make a "guest journey" poster for a guest, Mr Andre Thompson, who books a three-night stay, arrives late, has a nut allergy, reports a broken air conditioner on the second day and checks out early. For each stage (booking, before arrival, arrival, the stay, departure and after the stay), show which departments are involved, what each one does, and what information is passed on and to whom. Part 3: act out two short handovers: the front office telling housekeeping about an early arrival, and the front office reporting the air conditioner fault to maintenance. Each member takes charge of at least one department on the poster and plays a role in a handover. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the chart and the poster once for the whole group.
materials: Chart paper, markers, rulers and sticky notes
Assessor's card with the guest's details and the size of the hotel
Paper and pens for planning notes
A desk and phone set up for the handover role plays
photos: The planning notes, showing which member is responsible for each department
The guest journey poster being put together
checklist: Placed the departments and job titles correctly on the organisation chart
Showed correct reporting lines (who reports to whom)
Described correctly what their department does at each stage of the guest's stay
Showed what information is passed on and to whom, including the allergy and the fault
Communicated clearly and politely in their handover role play
Explained their part of the chart or poster to the assessor and answered a question on it
safety: Use scissors and markers carefully and keep the work area tidy
Keep walkways clear of chart paper and bags
Keep the role plays calm and polite

practical2.title: Plan and cost a villa weekend package, and promote it
practical2.brief: As a group, plan a weekend package for 6 guests at a villa, work out whether it will make a profit, and design a promotion for it. The assessor gives you a card with made-up costs in J$ (for example the cost of food and drink for each guest, airport transfers, a river tour, extra staff hours, and the villa's share of fixed costs such as electricity and insurance) and a target profit. Part 1: choose what the package includes, and list it. Part 2: work out the total cost, the cost per guest, and a selling price that meets the target profit; another member checks every calculation. Part 3: do a simple SWOT for the package. Part 4: design a flyer or a social media post on paper, with no real guests' photos, that describes the package and its price, showing "plus GCT at the current rate" if the card says the villa is registered for GCT. Each member leads at least one part, and the group presents the package to the assessor as if to the villa owner. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the costing sheet, the SWOT and the flyer once for the whole group.
materials: Assessor's card with made-up costs and the target profit
Paper for the SWOT, and card and markers for the flyer
A table and chairs for the presentation
photos: The list of what the package includes
The costing sheet with the total cost and the cost per guest
The selling price worked out, with the checker's initials
The finished flyer or social media post
The group presenting the package to the assessor
checklist: Chose sensible items for the package and listed them clearly
Worked out the total cost and the cost per guest correctly
Set a selling price that meets the target profit, showing the working
Checked another member's calculation and corrected any mistake
Gave sensible strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
Designed a clear, honest promotion with the correct price
Presented their part clearly and answered a question on it
safety: Use only made-up names, costs and pictures; do not use real guests' photos or details
Use scissors and craft knives carefully
Keep drinks away from calculators and papers
Keep the work area tidy so that nobody trips
